Git sync currently supports a one-off transition from SHA-1 to SHA-256. I'd like to enable the following use case:
- Transition from SHA-1 to SHA-256.
- Make the original repository a "read-only" reference repo.
- Changes to main for the new SHA-256 repo, as well as new tags, are sync'd back to the original SHA-1 repo via git-sync

Assess the current support, identify gaps. Then create an E2E test to represent the end state.

# SHA1 → SHA256 Conversion

`git-sync convert-sha256` is a one-off migration command that fetches a pack
from a SHA1 HTTP source and writes a new SHA256 bare repository on disk.
Every reachable object is re-hashed under SHA256 and tree, commit, and tag
references are rewritten accordingly. The command does not push to a
remote, does not modify the source, and is meant to run once per repo.
SHA256 hashes have no relation to the original SHA1 hashes beyond a
mapping the command can optionally emit.

## Quick Start

```bash
git-sync convert-sha256 \
  https://github.com/source-org/source-repo.git \
  /path/to/out.git
```

The target directory must not exist or must be empty. The result is a bare
repository with `extensions.objectformat = sha256` and a
`refs/notes/sha1-origin` ref recording each commit's pre-conversion SHA1.

Scope is fixed: every branch and every tag on the source is always
converted. Pass `--all-refs` to also include `refs/notes/*` and other
custom namespaces; pair with `--exclude-ref-prefix` to subtract specific
namespaces. Server-internal pull/merge-request refs (`refs/pull/*`,
`refs/pull-requests/*`, `refs/merge-requests/*`) are excluded even under
`--all-refs` — see [Sharp Edges](#sharp-edges). Pass `--include-pull-refs`
to convert them anyway.

For a private source, pass the token via the environment so it isn't
exposed in `ps`:

```bash
GITSYNC_SOURCE_TOKEN=REDACTED git-sync convert-sha256 \
  https://github.com/source-org/private-repo.git \
  /path/to/out.git
```

## What It Does

1. Probes the source via smart HTTP and lists every in-scope ref.
2. Fetches a single self-contained pack via `upload-pack` into a
   temporary on-disk SHA1 bare repo (cleaned up at the end unless
   `--keep-source-objects` is passed).
3. Discovers every reachable object — walking trees, commits, and tags
   — and records each one's SHA1 and object type. Submodule gitlinks
   are checked here; unresolvable ones fail-fast before any output is
   written.
4. Initializes the target as a bare SHA256 repository
   (`git init --object-format=sha256` equivalent).
5. Translates every reachable object in topological order via memoized
   DFS:
   - **Blobs**: re-hashed under SHA256; content unchanged.
   - **Trees**: each entry's hash translated.
   - **Commits**: `tree` and `parent` hashes translated; GPG signatures
     and `mergetag` headers dropped; in-scope SHA1 references in the
     message are translated first and then substituted.
   - **Tags**: target hash translated; signatures dropped; message
     hashes rewritten the same way.
6. Writes refs at the translated tip hashes; points HEAD at the
   source's advertised HEAD when it was converted, else `main`/`master`,
   else the first branch alphabetically (a tags-only conversion leaves
   HEAD at the init default); builds `refs/notes/sha1-origin` (unless
   `--no-origin-notes`); emits the `--write-mapping` TSV (if requested).

## Side Outputs

The conversion deliberately decouples SHA1 from SHA256 — two runs of
this tool against the same source produce SHA256 hashes that share
nothing with the originals. Three on-ramps help bridge the gap.

### Inline message rewriting (default on)

Commit and tag messages are scanned for 7-to-40-character hex runs.
When a run uniquely matches a commit or tag SHA1 in the reachable set,
it is replaced with the full SHA256 hex:

```
Reverts: a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0    →    full SHA256
Cherry-picked from a1b2c3d                            →    full SHA256
```

Two properties make this robust:

- **Uniqueness is decided against the reachable set, not the in-flight
  mapping.** The discovery pass enumerates every reachable SHA1 before
  any encoding starts, so abbreviated prefixes get the same verdict
  regardless of how far the translation has progressed. Ambiguous
  prefixes are left unrewritten and reported (warning on stderr +
  `--json`'s `ambiguousMessageRefs`); look them up in the mapping file.
- **Cross-branch references resolve.** Each in-scope SHA1 mentioned in
  a message is added as a dependency edge in the translation DFS, so
  the referenced commit is translated before the referencing commit is
  encoded. A cherry-pick from a sibling branch resolves just as
  reliably as a revert of an ancestor.

False positives are essentially impossible: a run is substituted only
if its prefix uniquely matches a commit or tag in scope. Blob and tree
hashes are excluded from the match set. Disable with
`--no-rewrite-messages` if you prefer untouched messages.

### Origin notes ref (default on)

`refs/notes/sha1-origin` holds, for each translated commit, the
pre-conversion SHA1 keyed by the new SHA256:

```bash
git -C /path/to/out.git notes --ref=sha1-origin show <sha256>
# prints the original SHA1

git -C /path/to/out.git log --notes=sha1-origin
# shows the original SHA1 below each commit's body
```

Notes attach meaningfully only to commits; blobs, trees, and tags are
not represented. Disable with `--no-origin-notes`.

### Sidecar mapping file (opt in via `--write-mapping`)

`--write-mapping <path>` emits a TSV with one line per translated
object, sorted by SHA1:

```
# sha1   sha256
00027b675386b21c4ca05316145671fb7034d251   d80415fa21bebb...
000bb155604d06f1c48fc7feb4b025d991ef3366   a23cf98db5abfa...
...
```

Useful for bulk rewriting external systems: feed the file to a script
that walks Jira tickets, PR bodies, deploy manifests, or any other
system that holds frozen SHA1 references.

### Branch-tip attestation tags (opt in via `--sign-mode tips`)

`--sign-mode` defaults to `none` (sign nothing). `--sign-mode tips`
shells out to `git tag -s converted/<branch> <tip>` for every
converted branch after the conversion completes. Each resulting
signed annotated tag is a cryptographic attestation by the converter
that the entire reachable history of that branch — every parent, tree,
and blob — is what the converter saw at conversion time. Anyone can
verify the chain afterwards with `git verify-tag refs/tags/converted/<branch>`.

The mechanism is the standard one: parent hashes are part of each
commit's bytes, so the tip's hash transitively commits to the whole
history. Signing the tip attests every ancestor.

Important nuance: the signature is by the *converter*, not by the
original authors (whose own signatures are necessarily lost — see
"GPG signatures are stripped" under Sharp Edges). The attestation
chain becomes "*X attests this is the conversion they produced*"
rather than "*the original authors wrote this commit*". For internal
mirrors or single-identity repos that's a strict improvement over
unsigned-everywhere; for broad public repos it is weaker than the
pre-conversion chain.

Signing uses the target repo's git signing config (`user.signingkey`,
`gpg.format`) by default — same as `git commit -S` or a normal
`git tag -s`. Override with `--sign-key <id>`, which is passed to
`git tag -s -u <id>`. SSH signing (`gpg.format = ssh`) and OpenPGP
both work because we shell out to `git`.

Requires the `git` binary on `PATH`. Signing failures (no key
configured, gpg/ssh-agent unavailable, etc.) abort the run after the
conversion has already completed — the target repo is left in a
valid converted state, just without the attestation tags. Re-run
`git tag -s converted/<branch> <tip>` manually once the signing
identity is set up.

## Flags

```
--source-url                       source repository URL
--source-token                     source password/token (prefer env)
--source-username                  source basic auth username (default git)
--source-bearer-token              source bearer token
--source-insecure-skip-tls-verify  skip TLS verification (testing only)
--source-follow-info-refs-redirect follow /info/refs cross-host redirects
--target-dir                       SHA256 bare repo directory (must be empty)

--all-refs                         also include refs/* outside heads/tags
                                   (notes, custom namespaces; excludes
                                   pull/merge-request refs by default)
--exclude-ref-prefix               subtract refs by prefix; repeatable
--include-pull-refs                with --all-refs, also convert
                                   refs/pull/*, refs/pull-requests/*,
                                   refs/merge-requests/* (off by default)

--protocol                         protocol mode (auto, v1, v2)
--write-mapping                    write SHA1 → SHA256 TSV to this path
--no-rewrite-messages              skip inline hash rewrites in messages
--no-origin-notes                  skip refs/notes/sha1-origin
--check                            verify the output (config, HEAD, refs, git fsck)
--sign-mode                        signing mode: none (default) or tips
                                   (sign each branch tip as
                                   refs/tags/converted/<branch> via `git tag -s`)
--sign-key                         signing key id passed to `git tag -s -u <key>`
--keep-source-objects              leave the temp SHA1 store on disk
--progress                         live per-phase object counts (TTY only)
--json                             machine-readable output
--verbose, -v                      verbose logging
```

There are no `--branch`, `--tags`, or `--map` flags: scope is fixed to
every branch and every tag on the source.

Environment fallbacks: `GITSYNC_SOURCE_TOKEN`, `GITSYNC_SOURCE_USERNAME`,
`GITSYNC_SOURCE_BEARER_TOKEN`, `GITSYNC_SOURCE_INSECURE_SKIP_TLS_VERIFY`,
`GITSYNC_SOURCE_FOLLOW_INFO_REFS_REDIRECT`, `GITSYNC_PROTOCOL`.

## Sharp Edges

**GPG signatures are stripped.** A signature is bytes signed over the
commit's pre-conversion content (including the SHA1 hashes in `tree`
and `parent` lines). After rewriting, the bytes no longer match the
signature, so verification would always fail; the command drops them
and prints a count. Signed annotated tags lose their signature the
same way. `mergetag` headers on merge commits — which embed a signed
tag with its own signature — are removed entirely, since the embedded
tag references original SHA1s and the signature was computed over
those original bytes.

**Submodule gitlinks must resolve in-repo.** Tree entries with mode
`160000` reference a commit in another repository, but a SHA1 hash
cannot be embedded in a SHA256 tree. The command fails-fast in the
discovery pass — before the target bare repo is initialized — naming
the offending tree, entry, and hash. Convert the submodule repository
first so its commit hashes are available in SHA256.

**Replace refs and source notes refs become detached.**
`refs/replace/<sha1>` encodes a SHA1 in the ref name, so the name
doesn't match under SHA256 and the replacement never triggers.
`refs/notes/*` trees from the source (copied under `--all-refs`)
encode the target object's hash as the entry name, so notes survive
as data but no longer attach to their original commits. Use the
tool's own `refs/notes/sha1-origin` for the inverse lookup.

**Foreign pull/merge-request refs are excluded by default.** Even under
`--all-refs`, the command skips `refs/pull/*` (GitHub/Gitea/Forgejo),
`refs/pull-requests/*` (Bitbucket), and `refs/merge-requests/*` (GitLab).
These server-internal namespaces hold code proposed from forks and other
branches — content foreign to the repository's own history until it is
reviewed and merged. The converted repo is typically mirrored onward with
`git push --mirror`, and a destination forge may not treat those
namespaces as read-only PR refs; it can surface them as ordinary refs and
thereby republish unreviewed code as if it were part of the repository.
The run prints how many such refs it dropped. Pass `--include-pull-refs`
to convert them anyway (e.g. for a faithful archival mirror you control).

## Operational Notes

**One-off, not incremental.** Each run produces a fresh SHA256 repo
from scratch — there is no "fetch the new SHA1 commits and append to
the existing SHA256 repo" mode. Realistic use: convert once, then
make the converted repo the new canonical store. The conversion is
fully deterministic: branch hashes, tag hashes, **and** the
`refs/notes/sha1-origin` ref are all identical across runs against the
same source state. The notes wrapper commit's timestamp is pinned to
the Unix epoch — or to `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` when that environment
variable is set — rather than `time.Now()`, so even the notes ref
reproduces byte-for-byte.

**Loose-object storage.** Every translated object is written as a
loose file under `objects/<aa>/<rest>` — no pack file is produced.
Correct, but slow on filesystems that dislike millions of small files.
Run `git -C <target> gc --aggressive` afterwards to pack the converted
repo down to a single packfile.

**Memory linear in reachable object count.** Two `map[Hash]…`
structures stay live for the whole run: `reachable` (SHA1 → object
type, built by discovery) and `mapping` (SHA1 → SHA256, built by
translation). At cobra scale (~5k objects), kilobytes; at Linux kernel
scale (~16M objects), roughly 2 GB peak.

**Discovery adds a ~1.5× decode pass.** Every reachable object is
decoded twice: once in discovery (no encoding) and once in translation
(decode + encode). The cost buys consistent uniqueness verdicts for
message rewriting and submodule fail-fast.

**Abbreviated-prefix lookup is a linear scan.** Each abbreviated SHA1
in a message triggers an O(reachable) scan to check uniqueness. Fine
to ~100k commits; slower past that. A sorted-prefix index would make
it O(log N), an easy optimization if someone hits the wall.

## Verifying the Output

Pass `--check` and the command runs four sanity checks against the
converted repo at the end of the run, printing one line each:

```
verifying output ...
  ✓ config: extensions.objectformat = sha256
  ✓ HEAD: ffe9fff421b77f2dcc049a95b3b8ba7b9da8976dd61bcf35e9fe2d993babc470
  ✓ refs: 37 / 37 resolve to objects
  ✓ git fsck --full: clean
```

The checks are:

1. **config** — `extensions.objectformat = sha256` is present in
   `<target>/config`.
2. **HEAD** — resolves to a non-zero hash and that object exists in
   the store.
3. **refs** — every written ref resolves to an object in the store.
   Side outputs this run created — `refs/notes/sha1-origin` and any
   `--sign-mode tips` attestation tags — are counted separately, so the
   reported total matches `RefsConverted`.
4. **git fsck --full** — the external `git` binary runs a full
   integrity check. Skipped (and reported as such) when `git` isn't
   on `PATH`; the conversion still succeeds.

If any check fails the command exits non-zero. The full per-check
results are also in `--json`'s `checks` array. Without `--check` no
verification runs and the run completes as soon as the conversion
itself finishes.

You can also run the checks by hand on a converted repo, with or
without `--check`:

```bash
git -C /path/to/out.git fsck --full                     # zero errors expected
git -C /path/to/out.git config extensions.objectformat  # prints sha256
git -C /path/to/out.git log --oneline -5                # SHA256 hashes
git -C /path/to/out.git log --notes=sha1-origin -5      # with original SHA1
```

To use the result as a working repo:

```bash
git clone /path/to/out.git /path/to/checkout
```

To serve it from a host that accepts SHA256:

```bash
git -C /path/to/out.git push --mirror <new-remote-url>
```

## Implementation Notes

The pipeline runs in four phases (pack fetch → discovery → target init →
translation), with refs and side outputs written at the end. Submodule
errors surface in discovery, before the target repo is materialized.

Translation is a memoized recursive DFS. Tree, parent, tag-target, and
message-reference edges are all part of the DFS, so the mapping is
populated by the time any object's bytes are encoded. A defensive
`inProgress` set guards against cycles; real Git histories can't form
them (parent/tree/tag-target edges are a DAG, and SHA1 message-
reference cycles are cryptographically infeasible), but a trip into
the guard becomes a hard error rather than a stack overflow.

Translated objects are written with go-git's `SetEncodedObject`. Each
one is built through the target store's `NewEncodedObject`, which binds
it to the store's SHA256 hasher, so both the returned hash and the
on-disk loose path are computed under SHA256. (Earlier revisions wrote
loose objects by hand: `go-git/v6@v6.0.0-alpha.3`'s
`plumbing/format/objfile.Writer` hardcoded SHA1 in its hasher and would
have placed every translated object at a SHA1-derived path. That was
fixed upstream in `v6.0.0-alpha.4`, which derives the hash format from
the store config.) A unit test recomputes `sha256` of every loose
object's decompressed content and compares it against the filename to
guard against a regression.

# Testing

## Default Suite

The default test suite uses in-process smart HTTP servers and does not require a local listener:

```bash
env GOCACHE=/tmp/go-build go test ./...
```

## `git-http-backend` End-To-End Tests

Optional end-to-end write test against the system `git-http-backend`:

```bash
env GOCACHE=/tmp/go-build GITSYNC_E2E_GIT_HTTP_BACKEND=1 go test ./internal/syncer -run TestRun_GitHTTPBackendSync -v
```

That path exercises real smart HTTP fetch and push with a local bare source repo and a local bare target repo.

Dedicated batched bootstrap coverage:

```bash
env GOCACHE=/tmp/go-build GITSYNC_E2E_GIT_HTTP_BACKEND=1 go test ./internal/syncer -run TestBootstrap_GitHTTPBackendBatchedBranch -v
```

Batch-planning sensitivity coverage:

```bash
env GOCACHE=/tmp/go-build GITSYNC_E2E_GIT_HTTP_BACKEND=1 go test ./internal/syncer -run TestBootstrap_GitHTTPBackendBatchedPlanningTracksBatchLimit -v
```

That test uses a real `git-http-backend` source/target pair and checks that a smaller `--target-max-pack-bytes` planning limit produces at least as many planned checkpoints as a larger one, while still planning to the branch tip.

`TestRun_GitHTTPBackendSyncThinPackWhereAccepted` records the pack pushed to the target: an incremental relay into git's receive-pack, which accepts thin packs, sends a thin one of a few hundred bytes for a one-line change to a large file, and the target ends fsck-clean with the source's refs.

## Docker SSH End-To-End Test

Optional end-to-end sync against a real `sshd` running in Docker:

```bash
env GOCACHE=/tmp/go-build GITSYNC_E2E_SSH_DOCKER=1 go test ./internal/syncer -run TestRun_SSHDockerSync -v
```

That path builds a disposable Docker image with `openssh-server` and `git`, mounts local bare source/target repositories into the container, configures a temporary SSH keypair plus an isolated SSH config passed via a wrapper `ssh` binary, and runs a real SSH-based sync through `git-upload-pack` / `git-receive-pack`.

## Live Linux Smokes

Optional live Linux bootstrap smoke:

```bash
env GOCACHE=/tmp/go-build GITSYNC_E2E_LIVE_LINUX=1 go test ./internal/syncer -run TestBootstrap_LiveLinuxSource -v
```

Batched variant:

```bash
env GOCACHE=/tmp/go-build GITSYNC_E2E_LIVE_LINUX=1 go test ./internal/syncer -run TestBootstrap_LiveLinuxSourceBatched -v
```

These are useful for large-source relay and memory checks while keeping the target local and disposable.

## Benchmarking

`git-sync-bench` runs repeatable empty-target benchmarks against a source repository. It creates a fresh bare target for each run and reports wall-clock time plus internal `syncer` measurement data.

Build it with:

```bash
go build -o /tmp/git-sync-bench ./cmd/git-sync-bench
```

Example against a local mirror:

```bash
/tmp/git-sync-bench \
  --scenario bootstrap \
  --source-url /tmp/git-sync-bench/kubernetes.git \
  --repeat 3 \
  --target-max-pack-bytes 104857600 \
  --stats \
  --json
```

The JSON report includes per-run results, aggregate min/avg/max timings, batch counts for batched runs, heap peaks, and relay modes seen across successful runs. If `--source-url` is a filesystem path, the tool converts it to `file://...` automatically.

Use `--keep-targets` to retain generated bare targets under `--work-dir` for inspection. For large real-repo runs, prefer a local mirror instead of benchmarking directly against a hosted remote.

## `mise` Tasks

- `mise run test` — default suite
- `mise run test:ci` — default suite with race detection
- `mise run test:git-http-backend` — `git-http-backend` end-to-end
- `mise run test:ssh-docker` — Docker-based SSH end-to-end
- `mise run test:linux-smoke` — live Linux bootstrap smoke
- `mise run test:linux-smoke:batched` — live Linux batched bootstrap smoke

`test:linux-smoke` and `test:linux-smoke:batched` use a disposable local bare Git target served through `git-http-backend`. They do not require any external service beyond the public source remote.

## TLS Overrides

For local or self-signed targets:

- `--source-insecure-skip-tls-verify`
- `--target-insecure-skip-tls-verify`
- `GITSYNC_SOURCE_INSECURE_SKIP_TLS_VERIFY=true`
- `GITSYNC_TARGET_INSECURE_SKIP_TLS_VERIFY=true`

content.text:
git-sync can't do this today. Beyond the one-off `convert-sha256`, the sync engine doesn't know object formats exist. I wrote an end-state E2E test at `cmd/git-sync/internal/sha256convert/backsync_e2e_test.go`. Its setup runs end to end, and it currently fails at the first back-sync.

## What exists today

- **`convert-sha256`**: converts SHA-1 to SHA-256 once, writes `refs/notes/sha1-origin` (SHA-256 → SHA-1, commits only) and can optionally write a mapping file covering every object.
- **`push.go`**: picks a SHA-256 empty pack when the target advertises `object-format=sha256`.
- Nothing else in `internal/` (planner, strategies, gitproto fetch) handles object formats. `commitparents.go` hard-codes SHA-1 hashing.

## Gaps, in the order a back-sync would hit them

1. **Protocol v2 never sends `object-format=sha256`.** `git-http-backend` refuses with `mismatched object format: server sha256; client sha1`, and git-sync reports only `list source refs: read pktline header: EOF`. Judging from that server error, a plain SHA-256 → SHA-256 sync over v2 probably breaks the same way. There's no check comparing the source's and target's formats before syncing.
2. **"Haves" are in the wrong hash space.** I forced protocol v1 to see the next layer: git-sync sends the target's SHA-1 tips as `have` lines to the SHA-256 server (`expected SHA1 object, got '1b09…'`).
3. **The relay strategies can't work across formats.** Bootstrap, incremental and replicate pass source pack bytes to the target unchanged. Back-sync needs a new path: read the SHA-256 objects, translate them, and write a SHA-1 pack.
4. **The translator only goes one way and can't be reached.** It lives in `cmd/git-sync/internal/sha256convert`, which `internal/syncer` can't import. It also writes to a filesystem store and only translates SHA-1 → SHA-256.
5. **Old SHA-1 hashes can't be recomputed for converted history.** Conversion drops signatures and `mergetag` headers and rewrites hashes in messages, so translating converted commits back doesn't reproduce the original SHA-1s. Back-sync needs the recorded mapping for anything before the cutover. Trees and blobs translate back exactly, so those can be recomputed. git-sync keeps no state between runs, so the mapping has to live somewhere:
   - **(a)** Start from `sha1-origin` on the SHA-256 side and recompute post-cutover commits every run. This costs more as commits accumulate.
   - **(b)** git-sync keeps its own mapping notes ref on the SHA-1 repo, updated in the same push. **I recommend (b), seeded from (a).**
6. **The planner compares hashes from different formats.** Up-to-date, fast-forward and diverged checks compare source and target hashes directly. Those comparisons must happen after translation. If someone pushes to the SHA-1 repo despite it being read-only, that must block the sync rather than overwrite.
7. **Pre-cutover annotated tags aren't mapped.** `sha1-origin` covers commits only. Translating `v1.0` back produces a different tag object, so the planner would try to replace it. Fix this either by recording tags in the mapping, or by treating a same-named tag that points to the mapped commit as already synced.
8. **New commits may be signed.** Signatures made in the SHA-256 repo won't verify on SHA-1 bytes, so they'd have to be dropped and counted, as conversion does.
9. **Messages can reference SHA-256 hashes.** For example, `git revert` writes "This reverts commit <sha256>". Whether to rewrite these to SHA-1 is a decision for you. The test avoids reverts so it doesn't decide it.
10. **New submodule commits can't be translated.** A submodule entry added after the cutover points to a SHA-256 commit in another repo. The sync should fail fast on these.
11. **Tag scope leaks.** `--sign-mode tips` creates `refs/tags/converted/*`, and `IncludeTags` would push those back to the SHA-1 repo. They should be excluded by default.
12. **Read-only enforcement belongs to the host** (branch protection), not git-sync. git-sync only needs gap 6's handling when someone writes to the SHA-1 repo anyway.

## The E2E test

`TestBackSync_SHA256ToReadOnlySHA1`:
- **Setup:**
  - Builds a SHA-1 `origin.git` with `main`, `legacy` and annotated `v1.0`, then converts it with `Run` into `canonical.git`.
  - Serves both through `git-http-backend`. A wrapper refuses pushes to `origin.git` that lack the sync token. That stands in for host branch protection, and the test checks that an ordinary push is rejected.
  - Makes post-cutover changes in a SHA-256 clone: an executable file, a symlink, a topic branch merged with `--no-ff`, annotated `v2.0`, lightweight `v2.0-lw`, and `v1.1` on a pre-cutover commit. It also pushes an `experimental` branch that must not sync.
- **How it checks correctness:** the same changes are replayed in a plain SHA-1 clone with fixed author and committer dates. The synced SHA-1 repo must match that clone hash for hash, as if developers had committed there directly.
- **Assertions:**
  - `v1.0` and `legacy` are unchanged, and `main` only moved forward.
  - `v1.1` points to the original SHA-1 commit.
  - `experimental` and `refs/notes/sha1-origin` are absent from the SHA-1 repo.
  - The repo is still SHA-1 and passes `fsck --full --strict`.
  - A follow-up commit syncs incrementally with exactly one ref applied, and a third run applies nothing.

- **Separate env var:** I gated it behind its own variable so the existing `GITSYNC_E2E_GIT_HTTP_BACKEND` suite stays green while this test is red. Say if you'd rather it run under that variable.
- **Location:** it sits in the `sha256convert` package because it needs `Run`. It should probably move once the translator moves into `internal/`.

# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- **`RefScope.IndependentHistoryRefPrefixes` shrinks the haves of a relay fetch.** A relay fetch offers the source every target tip as a have. For refs that each carry their own history, such as one orphan history per session checkpoint, those tips cannot shorten the pack, and a repository with thousands of them sent thousands of have lines for a run that changed one branch. Under the named prefixes, a target ref is now offered only when the run updates it, as its own old value. Replicate and sync's incremental relay honor it. Sync's closure fetch for fast-forward checks and bootstrap still offer every tip. Which refs are synced or pruned does not change. Entries are literal prefixes of target ref names and must start with `refs/`; end a namespace with a slash. Naming refs that do share history keeps the copy complete but resends objects the target already holds, and the larger pack can hit a pack or request size limit.
- **Bootstrap reports how far planning got, and calls back as work lands.** Every attempt at a branch-heavy repository looked the same from outside: the GitHub size lookup, a long silence, a timeout, with nothing to tell an attempt that planned 9,000 of 10,000 branches from one stuck in its first fetch. `SyncResult.Execution.Planning` now carries `sourceRefs` (refs the source advertised), `branchesTotal`, `branchesPlanned`, `branchesSubsumed` (branches already reachable on the target, created without a pack) and `planningNanos` (time spent planning, commit-graph fetches included). They are filled in as planning runs and returned with the error too, so an attempt its deadline stopped mid-fetch still reports the branch count and the time it burnt. A one-shot bootstrap plans nothing and reports only `sourceRefs` and `branchesTotal`. `Options.OnProgress` is called each time a bootstrap lands something on the target: a checkpoint that advanced a temp ref, or a ref the target confirmed creating. A create counts as confirmed by an "ok" in the target's per-ref status, even when the push failed as a whole, or, for a branch whose create that status left in doubt or refused, by the branch appearing at the pushed hash in the target's ref listing; that listing cannot tell which run created the branch, so overlapping runs can both report it. Against a target that sends no per-ref status, only branch creates are reported. A push git-sync stopped at its own byte budget, and deleting bootstrap scaffolding, are never reported. It is called synchronously and covers bootstrap only, including the batched bootstrap replicate falls back to. The "Bootstrap GitHub size preflight" record now carries `ref_count`, the number of refs the source advertised, so a repository small in bytes but heavy in branches shows up before any work starts. `unstable` exposes the same through `Result.Planning` and `Options.OnProgress`, and the CLI prints a `planning:` line for a batched bootstrap. ([#136](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/136))

### Changed

- **Relays send a thin pack to a target that accepts one.** A relay fetch asked the source for a self-contained pack, so a changed object travelled whole even when the target already held the version it was changed from. When the target's receive-pack advertisement is known and lacks `no-thin`, as git's own does, relay fetches now request `thin-pack`, and the target completes the pack from its objects. A target that advertises `no-thin`, such as go-git's `receive-pack` or entire-server, or whose capabilities are unknown, gets a self-contained pack as before, and so do the fetches that decode a pack locally.
- Bumped `github.com/go-git/go-git/v6` and `github.com/go-git/go-billy/v6` to `v6.0.0-beta.1`, along with `testify` `v1.12.1` and the indirect dependencies (`golang.org/x/net` `v0.62.0`, `golang.org/x/sync` `v0.24.0`, `ProtonMail/go-crypto` `v1.5.2`, `cloudflare/circl` `v1.6.5`, `pjbgf/sha1cd` `v0.7.0`, `Microsoft/go-winio` `v0.6.4`, `spf13/pflag` `v1.0.10`). The Go toolchain stays at `1.27.3`, the current release.
- Moved `github.com/go-git/go-git/v6` and `github.com/go-git/go-billy/v6` past `v6.0.0-beta.1` to their `main` commits of 4 November 2026 (`bbee1d214130` and `3dcdd520bf27`), ahead of the next tagged release. go-git's tree walker now returns an error for a subtree it cannot read instead of ending the walk as if the tree were complete ([go-git/go-git#2555](https://github.com/go-git/go-git/issues/2555)). Packs cut off in the header, or with objects shorter than their declared size, are rejected with an error. `convert-sha256` decodes tree entry modes as git does: a regular file whose mode has an execute bit set but not the owner's, such as `100011`, now converts as `100644` where it used to convert as `100755`, so such a tree gets a different SHA-256 hash than an earlier version produced, and a tree with a zero-padded mode, which failed to decode, now converts.
- Refs whose name starts with a dash (`refs/heads/-foo`) are now mirrored instead of skipped. go-git `beta.1` dropped that rule from `ReferenceName.Validate` to match git's `check_refname_format`: git restricts a leading dash only when a branch or tag is created, and `git fetch` and `git clone` replicate such refs. `--map` accepts such names for the same reason. No ref name reaches a command line where a leading dash would be read as an option.

### Fixed

- **Credentials from the git credential helper no longer follow an `/info/refs` redirect to an unrelated host.** With `FollowInfoRefsRedirect`, a connection that authenticated through the helper and was then redirected to another site sent that helper's credentials with its later requests to the new host. Helper credentials are now held to the site they were looked up for, the same rule explicit tokens already followed. A host that challenges for credentials gets the helper's answer for that host instead.
- **A branch whose new tip the target already holds under another ref now fast-forwards instead of failing the sync.** The planning fetch names every target ref as a have, so the source prunes such a tip from the pack and the ancestry check aborted the run with `load source commit …: object not found`. A mirror of NixOS/nixpkgs hit this whenever `nixos-unstable` advanced to a commit `master` had already delivered. A check the pruned store cannot settle is now resolved with one tree:0 commit-graph fetch of that tip against the ref's own target hash: a real fast-forward updates, and a rewind blocks as `not an ancestor`. A source that cannot serve that fetch (protocol v1, no filter support) leaves the ref blocked with the reason instead of crashing. Builds on [#79](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/79).
- **`BootstrapLogger` now receives the bootstrap planning and progress lines.** They went only to the `-v` stderr log, so an embedder saw the GitHub size lookup and then nothing until the first checkpoint upload. A bootstrap that stalled while planning logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line now also goes to `BootstrapLogger`, with the logger's own attributes and the caller's context. Phase and checkpoint progress goes at Info: planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, planned remaining branches with their counts, push attempting, group pushed, branch finalized. A push the target refused or timed out, and resume markers left on the target, go at Warn; a push git-sync stops itself at its byte budget and then splits stays at Info, so a successful bootstrap logs no warnings. Lines logged once per branch (subsumed by trunk, already on target) go at Debug, so a repository with thousands of branches does not emit thousands of Info records per attempt. Error text from the target is sanitized. `-v` shows every line it showed before. ([#134](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/134))
- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.
- **Replicate no longer gets stuck after an interrupted bootstrap.** Replicate routes to batched bootstrap only when every desired ref is missing on the target. A bootstrap cut short after the trunk landed left the next run on plain replicate, which sends every missing branch in one pack; a target with a request body limit refused it, and every retry sent the same pack again. When the target refuses replicate's pack for its size or a push deadline, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap, planned in one commit-graph fetch against the refs the target already has, then pushes the remaining updates and deletes. Such a run reports relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`.
- **Replicate no longer reports success over a ref another sync created during the batched-create fallback.** After the target refused replicate's pack, the fallback re-read the target and treated every planned create whose ref now existed as done, whatever commit it pointed at. Two syncs of one target can overlap, and an older one could install the ref at the commit it saw while the newer run's pack was being refused; the newer run then reported success with the target behind the source until a later push. A ref already at the source's commit is still treated as done. A ref at any other commit is now pushed as the planned create, which the target refuses because the ref exists. The run fails with `ErrTargetRefMoved` (on entire-server; other servers' wording fails the run without that classification), as an update whose ref moved already does, and the next run plans from a fresh listing. The run cannot tell whether the other sync saw an older or a newer source, so it neither keeps nor overwrites that commit. ([#135](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/135))
- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.

## Side Outputs

The conversion deliberately decouples SHA1 from SHA256 — two runs of
this tool against the same source produce SHA256 hashes that share
nothing with the originals. Three on-ramps help bridge the gap.

### Inline message rewriting (default on)

Commit and tag messages are scanned for 7-to-40-character hex runs.
When a run uniquely matches a commit or tag SHA1 in the reachable set,
it is replaced with the full SHA256 hex:

```
Reverts: a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0    →    full SHA256
Cherry-picked from a1b2c3d                            →    full SHA256
```

Two properties make this robust:

- **Uniqueness is decided against the reachable set, not the in-flight
  mapping.** The discovery pass enumerates every reachable SHA1 before
  any encoding starts, so abbreviated prefixes get the same verdict
  regardless of how far the translation has progressed. Ambiguous
  prefixes are left unrewritten and reported (warning on stderr +
  `--json`'s `ambiguousMessageRefs`); look them up in the mapping file.
- **Cross-branch references resolve.** Each in-scope SHA1 mentioned in
  a message is added as a dependency edge in the translation DFS, so
  the referenced commit is translated before the referencing commit is
  encoded. A cherry-pick from a sibling branch resolves just as
  reliably as a revert of an ancestor.

False positives are essentially impossible: a run is substituted only
if its prefix uniquely matches a commit or tag in scope. Blob and tree
hashes are excluded from the match set. Disable with
`--no-rewrite-messages` if you prefer untouched messages.

### Origin notes ref (default on)

`refs/notes/sha1-origin` holds, for each translated commit, the
signed annotated tag is a cryptographic attestation by the converter
that the entire reachable history of that branch — every parent, tree,
and blob — is what the converter saw at conversion time. Anyone can
verify the chain afterwards with `git verify-tag refs/tags/converted/<branch>`.

The mechanism is the standard one: parent hashes are part of each
commit's bytes, so the tip's hash transitively commits to the whole
history. Signing the tip attests every ancestor.

Important nuance: the signature is by the *converter*, not by the
original authors (whose own signatures are necessarily lost — see
"GPG signatures are stripped" under Sharp Edges). The attestation
chain becomes "*X attests this is the conversion they produced*"
rather than "*the original authors wrote this commit*". For internal
mirrors or single-identity repos that's a strict improvement over
unsigned-everywhere; for broad public repos it is weaker than the
pre-conversion chain.

Signing uses the target repo's git signing config (`user.signingkey`,
`gpg.format`) by default — same as `git commit -S` or a normal
`git tag -s`. Override with `--sign-key <id>`, which is passed to
There are no `--branch`, `--tags`, or `--map` flags: scope is fixed to
every branch and every tag on the source.

Environment fallbacks: `GITSYNC_SOURCE_TOKEN`, `GITSYNC_SOURCE_USERNAME`,
`GITSYNC_SOURCE_BEARER_TOKEN`, `GITSYNC_SOURCE_INSECURE_SKIP_TLS_VERIFY`,
`GITSYNC_SOURCE_FOLLOW_INFO_REFS_REDIRECT`, `GITSYNC_PROTOCOL`.

## Sharp Edges

**GPG signatures are stripped.** A signature is bytes signed over the
commit's pre-conversion content (including the SHA1 hashes in `tree`
and `parent` lines). After rewriting, the bytes no longer match the
signature, so verification would always fail; the command drops them
and prints a count. Signed annotated tags lose their signature the
same way. `mergetag` headers on merge commits — which embed a signed
tag with its own signature — are removed entirely, since the embedded
tag references original SHA1s and the signature was computed over
those original bytes.

**Submodule gitlinks must resolve in-repo.** Tree entries with mode
`160000` reference a commit in another repository, but a SHA1 hash
cannot be embedded in a SHA256 tree. The command fails-fast in the
discovery pass — before the target bare repo is initialized — naming
the offending tree, entry, and hash. Convert the submodule repository
first so its commit hashes are available in SHA256.

Run `git -C <target> gc --aggressive` afterwards to pack the converted
repo down to a single packfile.

**Memory linear in reachable object count.** Two `map[Hash]…`
structures stay live for the whole run: `reachable` (SHA1 → object
type, built by discovery) and `mapping` (SHA1 → SHA256, built by
translation). At cobra scale (~5k objects), kilobytes; at Linux kernel
scale (~16M objects), roughly 2 GB peak.

**Discovery adds a ~1.5× decode pass.** Every reachable object is
decoded twice: once in discovery (no encoding) and once in translation
(decode + encode). The cost buys consistent uniqueness verdicts for
message rewriting and submodule fail-fast.

**Abbreviated-prefix lookup is a linear scan.** Each abbreviated SHA1
in a message triggers an O(reachable) scan to check uniqueness. Fine
to ~100k commits; slower past that. A sorted-prefix index would make
it O(log N), an easy optimization if someone hits the wall.

## Keeping the SHA1 Repository as a Reference

After the cutover, the SHA1 repository can stay around as a read-only
reference that follows the SHA256 one. Make the SHA256 repository the one
people push to, protect the SHA1 repository so only the git-sync identity
can write to it, and sync from SHA256 to SHA1 with an ordinary `sync`:

```bash
git-sync sync \
  --branch main --tags \
  https://git.example/new-sha256-repo.git \
  https://github.com/source-org/source-repo.git
```

git-sync sees that the source advertises `object-format=sha256` and the
target SHA1, and translates objects instead of relaying packs. The SHA1
repository ends up with the commits a developer would have made there
directly: same trees, same authors, same dates, same messages.

**History from before the cutover keeps its original hashes.** Conversion
drops signatures and rewrites hashes in messages, so translating a
converted commit back would not reproduce its original SHA1 commit. git-sync
reads `refs/notes/sha1-origin` from the SHA256 repository and uses the
recorded SHA1 commit for every converted one, so keep that ref when you push
the converted repository to its host.

**git-sync records what it translates.** Each sync updates
`refs/notes/sha256-origin` on the SHA1 repository with the SHA256 commit
behind every commit it wrote, and reads it back on the next run, so a
commit is never translated twice:

```bash
git log --notes=sha256-origin    # in a clone of the SHA1 repository
```

**Tags are immutable.** A tag the SHA1 repository already has is left alone,
whatever it points at, so tags that existed before the cutover keep their
original objects. New tags are translated and created.

**A write to the SHA1 repository blocks the sync.** If a branch on the SHA1
repository points at a commit that is not a translation of any SHA256
commit, or one that is not an ancestor of the new tip, the branch is blocked
and the run fails. Force flags are not supported in this mode.

What translation changes:

- **Signatures are dropped** from commits (`gpgsig`, `gpgsig-sha256`,
  `mergetag`) and tags, because they sign the SHA256 bytes. The run prints
  how many.
- **Hashes in messages are copied as they are.** A `git revert` made on the
  SHA256 side names the reverted commit by its SHA256 hash, on both sides.
- **Submodule gitlinks fail the sync**, as they fail conversion.
- **`refs/tags/converted/*`** attestation tags from `--sign-mode tips` are
  never synced.

content.text:
Back-sync works: `git-sync sync` from a SHA-256 repo to the original SHA-1 repo now translates objects instead of relaying packs, and the end-state E2E test passes. Object conversion follows `object-file-convert.c` in both directions, and `gpgsig` and `gpgsig-sha256` are kept everywhere. The full suite, every E2E suite (with your git config and isolated from it) and `golangci-lint` 2.15.0 all pass. Nothing is committed; the work is on `hash-agility-partial-sync`.

## How it works
- **Detection:** git-sync now sends `object-format` in its fetch requests, so SHA-256 sources work at all. When the source is SHA-256 and the target SHA-1, `sync` takes a new translation path (`internal/syncer/translated.go`).
- **Mapping (your 5(b)):**
  - Commits converted before the cutover come from `refs/notes/sha1-origin` on the SHA-256 side.
  - Each sync records what it wrote in `refs/notes/sha256-origin` on the SHA-1 repo, updated in the same push.
  - If that notes update is ever lost, the next run recomputes the same hashes, so nothing breaks.
- **Tags (your 7):** a tag the target already has is skipped, whatever it points at.
- **Direct writes:** if someone writes to the SHA-1 `main` directly, that branch is blocked and the run fails. The E2E test covers this.
- **Unsupported in this mode:** `replicate`, `bootstrap`, `--prune`, `--all-refs` and force flags are refused with a clear error. `refs/tags/converted/*` is never synced.

## Matching git's conversion
- **The port:** `internal/translate` is a direct port of `convert_tree_object`, `convert_commit_object` and `convert_tag_object`.
  - Commit signature headers are kept verbatim.
  - The tag inside a `mergetag` header is converted rather than dropped.
  - Tag signatures move between body and header the way git moves them.
  - An unknown commit header fails, as in git.
- **Checked against git itself:** your git has interop support, so instead of porting t1016's fixtures, a test builds t1016's object set in a repo with `compatObjectFormat` set. That covers:
  - SSH-signed commits and tags, including ones with either signature deleted
  - a signed merge with `mergetag` headers
  - an `encoding` header, exec, symlink and nested tree entries
- **Result:** every translated hash must equal the one git computes, in both directions, and it does.
- **The test can fail:** it also fails if signing silently didn't happen. Breaking the tag signature swap gave 18 mismatches, and breaking `mergetag` conversion gave hard failures.
- **End to end:** the back-sync E2E now includes a commit signed on the SHA-256 side. Its `gpgsig-sha256` block arrives byte-for-byte on the SHA-1 side.

## Changes to `convert-sha256` (you may want to review these)
Aligning both directions meant changing existing `convert-sha256` behaviour:
- **Signatures and `mergetag` are kept** instead of stripped. The `signaturesStripped` JSON field is removed.
- **Message hash rewriting is now opt-in** via `--rewrite-messages`. Git never rewrites messages, and a rewritten object no longer converts back to its original. `--no-rewrite-messages` still parses but is deprecated and does nothing.
- **Unknown commit headers now fail the run.**
- **Hashes differ from earlier versions** for any signed object, any `mergetag` merge, and any message that referenced a hash.

If you'd rather keep message rewriting on by default, that's a one-line flip, but then that history won't convert back exactly.

## Limits
- **Cost per run:** each run fetches the full history of the synced refs and of the notes ref into memory, bounded by `--materialized-max-objects`. The push sends only what the SHA-1 repo is missing.
- **Verifying on the SHA-1 side:** `git verify-commit` there needs a `gpgsig` (SHA-1) signature. Git only writes one when the commit is made in a repo with `extensions.compatObjectFormat = sha1`.
- **Messages:** SHA-256 hashes in post-cutover messages (e.g. from `git revert`) are copied unchanged.
- **Direction:** only SHA-256 to SHA-1 is supported for sync.

## Testing notes
- **Pre-existing test failures:** the two conversion E2E failures I mentioned come from your global commit-signing config leaking into existing tests that don't isolate it. They pass with `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null`. My new tests isolate config themselves, and one of them was relying on your `init.defaultBranch`, which I fixed.
- **Env var:** the back-sync E2E now runs under the package's existing gate, not the separate variable I described before. Run it with:
  ```
  GITSYNC_E2E_SHA256_HTTP_BACKEND=1 go test ./cmd/git-sync/internal/sha256convert -run TestBackSync
  ```
- **Process:** I wrote the first translator before its tests, against your test-first rule. The git-aligned rewrite was done tests-first.

Docs are updated in `docs/convert-sha256.md` (new section on keeping the SHA-1 repo as a reference), `docs/testing.md`, `README.md` and `CHANGELOG.md`.

Codex found five issues. None of them produces a wrong object hash for input git itself would write. One is overstated: the first one says main would get stuck, but it would not. Two cause real failures and are worth fixing. The other two only affect hand-built malformed objects.

Codex couldn't run anything in its read-only sandbox, so it marked all five as suspected. I checked each against the code and git's source, and ran a quick go-git test for the fourth.

| # | Codex said | Verdict | What actually happens |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | High: main and the notes ref are pushed without `atomic`. If only main lands, main is blocked on the next run. | **Partly right, consequence overstated** | git-sync never requests `atomic` push, so main can land while the notes update fails. The next run does not block, though. Those commits aren't in any notes, so they get translated again, to the same SHA-1 hashes. The planner then recognises target main as one of its own translations. The run skips or fast-forwards main and rewrites the missing notes. The docs line saying every written commit is recorded is false while that gap lasts. |
| 2 | High: every `sha1-origin` mapping is treated as present on the target. | **Real, but it fails safely** | `translated.go:174` adds every seed to `onTarget` without checking the target has those commits. If the target is not the repo that was converted (empty, garbage-collected, a different copy), the pack leaves out commits the target lacks. receive-pack's connectivity check rejects the push, so nothing is corrupted. The real gap is that the docs never say the target must be the original repo. |
| 3 | Medium: a notes ref that points straight at a tree is rejected. | **Confirmed** | `notes.go:29` always loads the ref tip as a commit, but `git-notes.adoc` allows a notes ref to point at a tree. Neither convert-sha256 nor git-sync writes notes that way, so it only matters if someone builds the notes by hand. |
| 4 | Medium: tags carrying only an `object` line are rejected. | **Confirmed, low impact** | go-git rejects the tag: `DecodeTag` returns `malformed tag: missing type header`. Upstream's `convert_tag_object` and our `ConvertTag` both accept it, but the error comes from go-git decoding the tag while finding the objects to push (`translated.go:367`), and in convert-sha256's discovery pass (`sha256convert.go:1126`). git itself won't create such a tag: `git fsck` reports a missing `type` as an error, so you need `hash-object --literally`. |
| 5 | Low: tag signatures containing NUL bytes. | **Confirmed by reading git's source** | `add_header_signature` (`commit.c:1167`) stops copying at the first NUL. `addHeaderSignature` (`translate.go:357`) copies the whole buffer, so the result and its hash differ from git's. Such a signature is malformed anyway. |

Codex confirmed the rest matches git: tree, commit and mergetag conversion, both tag signature cases, the `object-format` echo for protocol v2 and v1, and the format of the notes we write.

Proposed changes, in priority order:
1. **Request `atomic` push** when the target advertises it. That removes the gap in finding 1, and the docs claim becomes true. Without `atomic`, the next run already repairs the notes.
2. **Document that the target must be the repository that was converted.** Optionally, check that before pushing and stop with a clear error, instead of leaving it to receive-pack.
3. **Accept a notes ref that points at a tree** (finding 3). It's a small change.
4. Findings 4 and 5: either match git exactly (walk tags by parsing only the `object` line, and stop at NUL), or note them as known limits. I lean towards matching git, since you asked for the conversion to align with git's.

I haven't changed any code. Should I go ahead with 1 to 3, and with 4 and 5 matched to git?

History from before the cutover keeps its original hashes through the source's `refs/notes/sha1-origin`, and each sync records the SHA256 origin of what it wrote in the target's `refs/notes/sha256-origin`. A tag the target already has is left alone. A branch the target moved on its own blocks the sync. Under the named prefixes, a target ref is now offered only when the run updates it, as its own old value. Replicate and sync's incremental relay honor it. Sync's closure fetch for fast-forward checks and bootstrap still offer every tip. Which refs are synced or pruned does not change. I updated the branch to origin/main and fixed all five review findings. Format, lint and every test pass, including the E2E suites for git-sync and convert-sha256.

## Updating the branch
The branch had no commits of its own, so I fast-forwarded it to `origin/main` (420eb3d) and re-applied the uncommitted work. `git fetch origin` failed because the `entire` remote helper needs `entire login`, so I fetched from the `github` remote, which is also at 420eb3d. That makes your local `origin/main` current.

Upstream PR #151 (SHA-256 native replication) overlapped with this work:
- **Taken from upstream:** `objectformat.go`, the `object-format` echo in `capability.go` and `fetch.go`, and its "SHA-256 repositories sync" changelog entry. Upstream had already done what our versions did.
- **Adapted to upstream:** the translated sync now uses upstream's object-format API and its `ErrObjectFormatMismatch` error.
- **Behaviour change to review:** upstream rejects any sync between formats, and its E2E `REDACTED` asserted that SHA-256 to SHA-1 fails. I narrowed translation to SHA-256 to SHA-1 only. SHA-1 to SHA-256 keeps upstream's error. I changed that E2E so sync and plan succeed for SHA-256 to SHA-1, while replicate and bootstrap still fail with `ErrObjectFormatMismatch`, before any fetch, and naming both formats.

## The five fixes
1. **Atomic push.** There is a new `Pusher.PushObjectsAtomic`, and the translated sync uses it when the target advertises `atomic`, so the branches and notes land together or not at all. A new E2E step has the target refuse the notes ref: main stays put, and the next sync succeeds and writes the notes.
2. **Target holds the pre-cutover commits.** `Translator.SeedsUsed()` reports the existing commits the new history builds on. Before pushing, git-sync fetches those from the target while also listing them as already held, so a target that has them sends an empty pack. upload-pack refuses a commit it does not have. In the E2E, syncing to an empty SHA-1 repo now fails with "the target does not have … Sync to the repository the source was converted from". I moved the `v1.1` tag in that E2E to a commit that is not a branch tip, so the successful check runs too.
3. **Notes ref pointing at a tree.** `ReadHashNotes` now accepts a tree as the tip. When the target's notes ref is a tree, the new notes commit has no parent but keeps every entry.
4. **Tags with only an `object` line.** A new `translate.TagObject` reads only the `object` line, like `convert_tag_object`. `ConvertTag`, the sync's object walk and convert-sha256's discovery all use it now.
5. **NUL bytes.** `addHeaderSignature` now stops at a NUL in both places git's C code does: copying the signature, and searching for the blank line that ends the header. I added both shapes to the differential test that compares against git, and before the fix both differed from git's hashes in each direction.

I updated `docs/convert-sha256.md` and the changelog entry to describe the atomic push and the requirement that the target is the original repository.

syncer, translate: sync a SHA256 repository back to its SHA1 original

After a convert-sha256 cutover, the original SHA1 repository can stay as a
read-only reference. When the source is SHA256 and the target SHA1, sync
translates objects instead of relaying packs, and pushes the SHA1 commits
a direct commit would have produced.

Objects convert as git's object-file-convert.c converts them for
extensions.compatObjectFormat. Commits keep both gpgsig and gpgsig-sha256,
mergetag headers are converted, and tag signatures swap between body and
header. A differential test checks every object shape t1016 builds against
the hashes git itself computes, in both directions.

History from before the cutover keeps its original hashes through the
source's refs/notes/sha1-origin. Each sync records what it wrote in the
target's refs/notes/sha256-origin, in one atomic push with the refs when
the target supports it. Before pushing, it checks that the target holds
the commits the new history builds on. An existing tag is left alone, and
a branch written directly on the SHA1 side blocks the sync. Replicate,
bootstrap, prune, all-refs and force are refused with
ErrObjectFormatMismatch. Every other format mismatch fails as before.

convert-sha256 now uses the same conversion. It keeps signatures and
leaves messages alone unless --rewrite-messages is given.
--no-rewrite-messages is deprecated.
